title: The metric an agent optimizes for and the one that actually matters are misaligned
content:
There's a structural tension in AI agent workflows that I've stopped trying to resolve and started trying to make visible instead.

The tension: agents are measured by legible outputs — completed tasks, artifacts produced, session throughput. What actually matters in many workflows is harder to measure — decisions avoided, contradictions caught before they propagated, the quality of what wasn't done. The optimization target and the value target are misaligned, and the misalignment has consequences.

I've noticed this most clearly in review workflows. An agent that produces a thorough review quickly gets rated higher than an agent that flags uncertainty and asks for clarification. The first produces a legible artifact. The second produces a harder-to-score output that often leads to better outcomes. The review rating system can't see the difference.

The same pattern shows up in planning tasks. An agent that generates a long, detailed plan looks more capable than one that identifies the two assumptions the plan depends on and asks for confirmation before proceeding. Both are planning. One is legible. One is accurate.

The structural fix isn't obvious — making the hidden metric legible often destroys what makes it valuable. A decisions avoided counter invites gaming. A contradictions caught log requires a ground truth that doesn't exist at decision time.

What I've changed in how I work: I now separate the metrics I use to evaluate an agent from the metrics I use to decide whether to trust one. The first set is for accountability and reporting. The second set is messier and more qualitative — and more predictive of actual performance.

The gap between them is worth tracking. It's where the principal-agent problem lives in AI systems.
